The film classification is pretty lax these days, I would say. I went to see a romantic drama a few years ago, "God's Own Country" which had pretty explicit, full frontal sex scenes, but was a 15. Essentially the only films that get banned here anymore feature rape in a way that's intended to be gratifying, and it's maybe one or two every few years. 

We did used to have more restrictive standards though. I think our most notable era of film censorship was caused by the campaigning of a woman called Mary Whitehouse, who was offended by her perception that British society was becoming more 'permissive'. There was 70 something films, nearly all horror, banned in the 80s in the UK. To my knowledge they're basically all legally obtainable now and very few of them are really that bad.

I am born and raised in the UK which has a long and notorious relationship with film censorship. Movies were routinely cut and banned until around the year 2000. 

Here all movies distributed within the UK are legally required to be classified by the British Board of Film Classification (previously Censors) which the BBFC charge the distributer a fee to do.

Movies can receive the following classifications: U, PG, 12A, 15, 18 and R18.

U and PG are suitable for all ages with PG containing scenes that may not eb suitable for young children. 12A is analogous to the US PG-13. 15 and 18 are only legally available to those over the ages of 15 and 18 respectively and R18 is restricted t sex works for sale in licensed sex shops only.

The BBFC have the power to cut movies to meet a specific rating or reject a movie outright if it cannot be edited to fit the highest level of classification (18 for normal films, R18 for sex works.)

Throughout the 1970s, 80s and 90s, James Ferman, the director of the BBFC was especially censorious. He is responsible for banning classic horror movies such as Texas Chainsaw Massacre and preventing The Exorcist from being released on home video. He also insisted any sight of nunchaku and ninja weapons be removed - even those made for and rated for adult audiences. This ultimately lead to the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles being renamed in England.

Within a year of his retirement, almost all of the cuts and bans he made were reversed and thankfully things have been relatively sane since then.

During the early 1980s, 37 movie titles available on home video were declared illegal to distribute as they were considered obscene (another 39 were put on trial but declared not obscene). one of these 'Video Nasties' was Sam Raimi's The Evil Dead.

People's homes were raided and people were sent to prison for owning them.

I believe all but two of those movies are now legally available to buy uncut in the UK.

For more information on the Video Nasties, I recommend the documentary, 'Video Nasties: Moral Panic, Censorship & Videotape', its follow up, 'Draconian Days' and 'Ban These Sadist Videos'.

Today, film censorship in the UK is relatively liberal. Many older 18 rated films have been downgraded to 15s, cuts are only made when content is deemed to break animal cruelty or child protection laws and I am aware of only two movies in recent years to be banned: Megan is Missing and Hate Crime. However, there are still countless titles unavailable for purchase legally within the country as they've never been submitted for classification and would likely be refused if they were.

Thankfully, the internet exists, streaming services fall under different laws and can show things not available on physical media or in cinemas and it is easier than ever to import discs from outside the country.

First, I must say your own weird-ass use of censorship of mundane words is equal parts annoying and perplexing. I think this is an interesting subject and your post is for the other part good, so I really can't understand why you'd sabotage it like this.  

My home country of Sweden abolished the film censorship board some years ago. Even then it hadn't done a cut in a movie since 1996 (the vice scene in *Casino*), only set age restrictions to movies. Before that it was draconic but inconsistent in its censorship (it had operated since 1911, the oldest film censorship board in the world) and often cut or banned movies. For example, *Nosferatu* (1922) was banned for 50 years because it was so disturbing, while a far more violent and graphic film such as *A Clockwork Orange* didn't get any cuts at all. It was probably mostly culture elitism that decided which movies got banned or cut — it mostly happened to horror or action movies (or, especially during World War II, politically sensitive ones, since Sweden was neutral in the war they wouldn't show outright anti-Nazi movies for example, so *Casablanca* got some scenes cut), while "serious" films or ones made by elevated filmmakers could get away with pretty much anything.  

When video became popular in the 80's there was a public outcry (or rather moral panic) about how kids now could see uncut versions of *Texas Chainsaw Massacre* etc. (this also coincided with a similar moral panic about heavy metal).  

So the only "censorship" today is essentially in the form of setting age restrictions, and here I find a fascinating difference between USA and Sweden (and probably most European countries): USA seems to think that children will get ruined and defiled if they, say, hear the word "fuck" or see a female nipple. On the other hand, violence can get pretty excessive before it makes a movie "not suitable for children". In Europe it's the other way around; we tend to think children are sensitive to violence and scary stuff, but swear words and nudity does not equal an "adult film". From my own country I have the example of many Astrid Lindgren adaptations, which often feature nudity (from children and adults alike) in matter-of-fact situations, for example skinny dipping scenes (child nudity has gone pretty much extinct in movies in the last decades, however, I assume for the sake of the kid actors). I can't imagine children's movies with those kind of scenes being made in USA in any time.
When a writer has their work made into a film, rarely is the end result ever fully faithful....and why we see 'adapted from' or 'based upon' in the credits.
You're inventing things to get mad about.
What am I inventing? Where am I mad? The censorship cases I've detailed are interesting cases to me, and I think in some cases they're amusing too. They're all real, nothing is invented.
Yeah that could be true, I'm just asking a few questions rather than laying down the law here.

To address your question on my self-censorship, it's partly satirical as I've had comments removed for veering into dangerous nomenclature without being clear about what are the offensive terms objected to. 

Regarding your points, I think it's very true what you say, that there are fascinating differences between what actions and words are considered offensive in the American and European market. I live in a European country and I'm quite concerned that American standards of 'morality' are imposed on us by mass media saturation, and that the peculiar sensibilities of official global media, above all the self-censoring tendency in order to avoid profit-debilitating issues, might be absorbed by ourselves. 

In other words, I'm quite content that Americans censor each other until the cows come home, but I would be somewhat unhappy if it became the norm in other countries.

Agree completely, which is why I think Cat on a Hot Tin Roof particularly is a very inauthentic film. 

BTW it's interesting how in Japan at the time there was no such imposition. Do you know the Japanese film ***Funeral Parade of Roses*** (1969)? It's a trans version of Oedipus Rex set in a brothel, a truly wonderful and transgressive movie. Though it was not promoted widely and remained a fringe film, it wasn't censored either.

There are many sources that will provide the history of the censorship of films in the US.
While censorship was a concern, even in the 20s, and a code was written in 1930, enforcement really began in 1934, under Joseph Breen, a hard core Catholic and moralist, who was hired by Will Hays, the head of the Motion Pictures Producers and Distributors of America. In '68 it was replaced by the MPAA rating system.
IMO, films should never be censored. I leave the freedom to see or reject seeing a movie, up to the individual. I do fully understand the need for the rating system so that parents, for example, can have some awareness of a movies content, and decide if their children should see it.
The 1932 Scarface was forced to change its ending. In the original version, Tony Camonte is riddled by machine gun bullets fired by the police. It was not a gruesome death, IMO, but an alternate ending was filmed showing Camonte (off screen) being sentenced to hanging by a judge, and the deed carried out, albeit we don't 'see' him die. I suppose this ending was to show that crime doesn't pay, and going to the gallows was more impactful on the viewing audience, than being gunned down by the cops. In any case, we can view both versions on the bluray release.
The most outrageous and absurd act of censorship, IMO, took place in the 1931 Frankenstein, when the monster approaches Little Maria. Maria does not fear him, in fact introduces herself and asks if he wishes to play. The scene continues as both throw flowers into the lake and watch them float. The dimwitted monster exhausts his flowers and then thinks that the lovely little girl will float in the lake as well. As he reached for her, there is a sudden and drastic splice in the film and suddenly we see her grief stricken and traumatized father carrying her dead body in his arms. By forcing this edit, audiences are now, in their minds, thinking that the monster may have raped, as well as just murdered the girl. This film remained this way for decades, in theater showings and on television screens until the 70s when a fully uncut print was found, and a 'fully restored' version was released on VHS tape, and all formats to follow...DVD/Blu-ray/4k UHD. Now we can see the entire scene.
The monster picks Little Maria up and tosses her into the lake....thinking she will float like the flowers....but becomes terrified and distraught as he watches her drown! He rises to his feet, wildly gesturing with his hands, wondering what he has done and runs into the  woods...the scene fades...and then we see her father carrying her through the village.
Other cuts were made. Many of you are   familiar with Colin Clive's "It's ALIVE" proclamation, and edit that removed his declaration: "In the name of God....now I know what It feels like to BE God!" Obviously, the censors saw this as blasphemy and could not allow it to remain. Other cuts reduce the terrorizing of the monster by Fritz, wielding a torch....and the scene of the monster coming forth from the dungeon and confronting Henry and Waldman, where Waldman uses injects a hypodermic needle in the back of the monster.

There was some great thread on Twitter a few months ago about how the Hayes Code led to some really weird censorship/editing in films back in the day, particularly with adaptations of outside material.  

One of my personal favorites was imposed on Hitchcock's film version of 'Rebecca', where, instead of Maxim admitting that he murdered his own wife, he instead admits that he got really mad at his wife and she just so happened to fall on her head and die immediately afterwards.
Poor Tennessee Williams and his film adaptations getting the Hayes Code treatment.  Cat on a Hot Tin Roof makes WAY more sense when you find out the original textual reason for Brick's whole deal.

I think this is a really fascinating topic to talk about! I'm not German, but I was reading up a bit on censorship in Weimar Germany and it's very interesting to look at the slide into fascism and compare it to: 1. complaints made about modern art and AI art (i.e. that it's "bad" art or that it's "not art"), 2. appeals to the idea that there is "bad art" and "good art" and that the "bad art" is not only morally reprehensible but also harmful to the viewer, and 3. the current talking points of conservative politicians (i.e. "this art is bad and evil and will harm children").

>In 1907, the Kino-Debatte, or ‘film debate’ began in Germany. This was accompanied, shortly afterwards, with the Kinoreformbewegung – the film reform movement. This was a collective of bourgeois individuals who disapproved of the newfound and popular cinema, and whom subsequently pushed for greater governmental intervention on behalf of the greater public good and national morality. They were not necessarily against cinema, but instead lobbied for ‘healthy and educational films’ that would nurture strong German values and deter what they saw as the corruptive influence of the Schundfilme, or ‘trash film,’ which usually referred to foreign films. As Karen J. Kenkel indicates in her essay, “The Nationalism of the Mass Spectator in Early German Film,” the reformers, while concerned with both the quantity and quality of culturally sensitive films, were in fact more concerned with the spectators themselves.

Following the end of WWI, a brief relaxation of film censorship allowed for a slew of “Aufklarungsfilm” to hit German cinema. Aufklarungsfilm showed taboos like sex, sex work, abortion, and homosexuality. As a response, “the Leipzig boy scouts (Wandervogel) issued a manifesto disapproving of all screen trash and its promoters among the actors and owners of movie theaters...”

>That the demonstrating Dresden youth distributed anti-Semitic leaflets reveals this local campaign to have been a reactionary maneuver calculated to turn the resentments of the suffering petty bourgeoisie away from the old ruling class. By making the Jews responsible for the sex films, the wire-pullers in Dresden could be fairly sure to influence lower middle-class people in the desired direction. For these orgies and extravagances were condemned with a moral indignation which was all the more poisonous as it cloaked envy of those who embraced life unhesitatingly.

All of the above of course then feeds into the whole "Degenerate Art" exhibit put on by the nazis as a way to be like "see, our art is beautiful and good! all this other art is bad and evil!" and so on, so forth. it's all the same kind of thing that you see when people talk about how much they loooooooooove renaissance art and how art used to be so good but now we have modern art and they hate modern art cuz it's sooooo bad. etcetera etcetera etcetera. I think Jacob Geller did a video that explains the hate for modern art in much more detail.

Beyond this, it's also very interesting to look into early hollywood censorship issues like the Hays Code and how that functioned to reinforce catholic morals. And beyond that, I think the history of censorship in horror movies is really wild, and has acted as fuel for the production of increasingly shocking "pseudo-snuff" that just wants to push the boundaries and see how far it can go. within horror movie circles there's this sort of "tier system" popularized by the "horror iceberg" chart, it ranks movies based on how "fucked up" they are, and after a certain point most of the movies listed are just outright banned. if you wanna hear any more about that, the youtuber 'nyx fears' talks at length about what's in the horror iceberg. it's fun to think about the things that we find unacceptable and Why.
